newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ PENSION FUND EARNINGS TAX TO STAY AT 33 PCT.
newsitem.headline: NZ PENSION FUND EARNINGS TAX TO STAY AT 33 PCT.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters and Revenue Minister Bill Birch on Wednesday released a discussion document detailing announced changes to the taxation of income from superannuation and life office funds.
Under the system, the tax rate on superannuation fund and life office earnings will remain at a flat 33 percent.
The document, called The Tax Credit System, says even though the tax rate will remain flat, funds will be able to choose to offer tax credits.

"In that case, savers would be able to have tax credits allocated to them for the tax paid by their fund on their behalf. That would allow their investment income to be taxed at their personal income tax rates," Peters and Birch said in a statement.
The tax credit system will also be available for funds under the proposed compulsory Retirement Savings Scheme, should it receive a 'yes' vote from the public in September's referendum.
"For low and middle income earners, that will, in effect, lower the target savings level, and make it easier for them to reach that level," the statement said.
Peters and Birch said the government aimed to introduce measures that allowed savers to pay income tax on their return from savings at the correct tax rate.
It wanted a workable solution by April 1, 1998.

"If it turns out that the tax credit system cannot be made available by then, we will consider adopting, as a temporary measure, a flat tax rate lower than 33 percent, until the tax credit system is available," Peters and Birch said.
They said they hoped to be able to introduce the necessary legislation into parliament in early 1998.
At present, superannuation funds and life offices, on behalf of savers, pay a flat and final tax rate of 33 percent on income earned by the fund.

Peters and Birch said that rate disadvantaged low-income and middle-income savers, whose other income was taxed at a lower rate. The government favoured the tax credit system as a means of resolving that problem.
Interested parties had until September 12 to make submissions on the proposal.
